claims.claim: OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology frames archaeology as the field that studies past societies through artifacts and other material remains, and its methods chapter presents scientific archaeological techniques as the foundation for studying the human past; Britannica defines archaeology as the scientific study of past human life and activities through the examination of material remains.

The archaeological record is classified into artifacts (portable objects showing evidence of human cultural activity, such as stone tools and pottery), features (non-portable cultural structures found at a site, such as hearths, house foundations, altars, and tombs), and ecofacts (natural objects found at a site, such as seeds, shells, and animal bones, showing no sign of human craftsmanship).

Archaeologists work at sites — bounded places where the material remains of past human activity are found — and across landscapes, the wider regions of fields, trails, roads, and settlements around and between sites; surveys to locate remains may be done on foot or with technologies such as drones and satellite imagery.

The three main fieldwork tools are survey (systematic search for surface remains without digging), excavation (systematic digging of a site in a grid, layer by layer, with every object documented and mapped in place before removal), and dating.

Dating methods include stratigraphy (relative dating by the law of superposition — deeper layers were deposited earlier and are older; the principle was proposed by Nicolas Steno in 1669), radiocarbon dating (measurement of carbon-14 decay in organic material such as wood, bone, and seed, usable back roughly 50,000 years), and dendrochronology (dating wood by counting annual tree rings and matching patterns across timbers).

Objects carry meaning through context: an object's primary context is where it lay undisturbed (in situ), the stratum it lay in, and the objects associated with it; an object moved before documentation loses its archaeological context, so careful documentation is the foundation of archaeological practice.

The archaeological record is a partial sample of past life: durable materials such as stone, fired clay, bone, and shell are what typically survive and are examined, while perishable materials such as wood, cloth, and food generally decay, so the record is incomplete — most of the past is gone.

Archaeology is often described as the closest thing to time travel: it cannot observe the past directly, but it reconstructs, orders, and interprets past societies from material remains, making the past physical and touchable.

Unlike historians, who work primarily from written texts, archaeologists study all aspects of past societies' material culture, from the earliest stone tools to recently buried or discarded objects; for periods without writing, material remains are the only record.

positions: The task brief permits attribution to AAA or OpenStax. The American Anthropological Association's pages could not be read this session: americananthro.org serves a JavaScript challenge to automated fetch, and the available Wayback captures of AAA pages render as JS shells without article content.

OpenStax's four-field framing ('past societies explored through artifacts') and methods chapter, plus Britannica's one-sentence definition ('the scientific study of past human life and activities through the examination of material remains'), were both verified by direct reading.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the working definition to OpenStax (per the sibling what-is-anthropology precedent) and notes Britannica corroboration; no AAA-specific wording is quoted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Section numbering discrepancy between the OpenStax canonical book and the LibreTexts mirror.
positions: The LibreTexts mirror labels the archaeological methods section '2.02: Archaeological Research Methods'.

The canonical OpenStax book numbers the same section 2.1; its canonical URL is https://openstax.org/books/introduction-anthropology/pages/2-1-archaeological-research-methods (confirmed via Wayback capture 20260416052902; the direct openstax.org fetch returns HTTP 404 to non-JS clients).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The canonical OpenStax URL (2-1-archaeological-research-methods) is registered in the source record; content was read via the LibreTexts mirror, and the notes state which copy was read.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Verbatim support for the honest note that 'most of the past is gone.'
positions: No consulted source states the phrase verbatim.

The sources support the underlying facts: the record consists of durable materials (stone tools, pottery, bone, shells) and the key-terms and methods chapter describe which categories of remains are found and examined.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The claim is marked INTERPRETIVE and presented in the lesson as the discipline's honest framing, grounded in the sources' descriptions of the record rather than quoted from them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Radiocarbon dating range stated differently in two sections of the same OpenStax chapter.
positions: Section 2.1 states the method is valid for organic samples between about 300 and 50,000 years old, with a margin of error near 50 years.
The chapter glossary (2.8) states radiocarbon is the most widely used technique for organic artifacts between about 50 and 60,000 years old.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says radiocarbon 'reaches back tens of thousands of years' without quoting either figure, and the evidence notes record both figures.

sourceRecords.title: 2.1 Archaeological Research Methods — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (2022 edition; 2026 captures display CC BY-NC-SA with a no-LLM-training notice)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. Canonical URL confirmed against a Wayback capture (web.archive.org/web/20260416052902/...), titled '2.1 Archaeological Research Methods'; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so content was read 2026-08-22 via the LibreTexts CC BY 4.0 mirror (section 2.02: Archaeological Research Methods; authors Jennifer Hasty, David G. Lewis, Marjorie M. Snipes). Supports: archaeology as the scientific study of the human past through material remains; survey as the first fieldwork step (walking fields, drones, Google Earth, test pits, GPS coordinates); excavation procedure (grid system, in situ recording, trowels and brushes, catalog numbers, soil and pollen samples); artifacts, features (trails, roads, house pits), and ecofacts with specialists (zooarchaeologists, archaeobotanists); primary vs secondary context and why documentation matters; the law of superposition (proposed by Nicolas Steno, 1669) and stratigraphic superposition; typological sequences and seriation (Flinders Petrie); chronometric dating: radiocarbon (carbon-14 in organic material, roughly 300-50,000 years, ~50-year margin), uranium and potassium-argon decay for non-organic materials, and dendrochronology (annual tree rings, cross-dating, wooden structures); triangulating several dating methods. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Ch. 2 Key Terms — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. Chapter glossary read 2026-08-22 via the LibreTexts CC BY 4.0 mirror (section 2.08: Key Terms). Supports the definitions used in the lesson: artifacts (portable objects showing evidence of human cultural activity — stone tools, pottery), features (non-portable cultural structures — parts of a temple, altars, tombs), ecofacts (natural objects at a site — seeds, bone, shells — with no sign of human craftsmanship), archaeological excavation, archaeological context, primary context, law of superposition, relative dating, radiocarbon dating (most widely used technique for organic artifacts between roughly 50 and 60,000 years old), dendrochronology (tree-ring growth patterns and cross-dating). Vocabulary definitions in the lesson are original prose informed by this glossary.

Article by Glyn Edmund Daniel, last updated July 10, 2026. Supports: archaeology as the scientific study of past human life and activities through the examination of material remains; artifacts from the earliest stone tools to recently made man-made objects; survey to locate sites and features (aerial photos, satellite images); excavation as exposure, recording, and recovery of buried remains (trowels, brushes); stratigraphy (older layers lower) as relative dating and radiocarbon dating of organic materials as absolute dating; archaeologists studying material culture while historians focus on written texts.
